design_detail: Cross-sectional anonymous questionnaire survey (June–December 2004) of 116 Australian residents aged 18 or over who had used ecstasy at least once, recruited by convenience and snowball sampling among people known to the researchers (98 questionnaires handed out) and through an advertisement on an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (thanked in the acknowledgements: RaveSafe and Pill Reports), with no record of which route each return came from. Self-completed questionnaire (about 15 minutes, closed and open questions) on demographics, ecstasy use, use of 15 other substances before, during and after ecstasy, pill testing, strategies endorsed from a list to avoid side effects, the 'comedown' and neurotoxicity, and preloading and postloading (pharmaceuticals and natural products taken before or after ecstasy). Descriptive percentages, with t-tests and chi-square tests of correlates. The effectiveness of the practices was explicitly not studied.
can_establish: Which practices before, during and after ecstasy use this self-selected Australian sample reported in 2004 (drinking water, limiting use, breaks, pill testing, preloading and postloading with vitamins, 5-HTP, magnesium and other products, other drugs taken alongside), and which respondent characteristics went with preloading and postloading in it.
cannot_establish: How common these practices are among people who use ecstasy in Australia or elsewhere (convenience and website sample, unknown response rate); whether any practice reduces harm (efficacy was not studied); how often each strategy was used (not asked); or whether the correlates are causes (cross-sectional, about 30 uncorrected tests).

sample.recruitment: Convenience and snowball sampling among people known to the researchers (98 questionnaires distributed) and an advertisement with a downloadable questionnaire on an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (RaveSafe and Pill Reports, named in the acknowledgements); questionnaires returned anonymously, so the split between the two routes is unknown (p. 169, Method 2.2; p. 175, Acknowledgements).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Australian residents aged 18 or over who had used ecstasy at least once in their lives (p. 169). Data collected June to December 2004.
sample.demographics: 51.3% women; age 18 to 41, mean 26.5 (SD 5.6); 82.5% born in Australia; 50.4% from Victoria, 18.3% New South Wales, 17.4% Western Australia, 10.4% Queensland, 2.6% South Australia, 0.9% Tasmania; 85.1% completed secondary school and 68.2% had further qualifications; 70.2% working and 21.9% studying (p. 170, Results 3.1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single questionnaire). The number of respondents varies between analyses (101 to 116) without a statement on missing answers.
sample.selection_effects: No sampling frame: acquaintances of the researchers, their networks, and readers of harm-reduction websites. The authors note that respondents found through the Internet may have a particular interest in harm reduction, which would inflate the reported use of harm-reduction practices, and that representativeness cannot be determined (p. 173). Most respondents used recently (79.1% in the past 3 months) and planned to use again (91.2%).

exposure.measurement: Self-report on an unvalidated questionnaire: ecstasy use (age at first use, frequency, usual and highest number of pills, years of use, route, place); use of 15 other substances and whether each was used before, during or after ecstasy; strategies endorsed from a list for three purposes; preloading and postloading, with substances, frequency, sources and reasons in open questions (pp. 169–170, Method 2.3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported pattern of the sample (p. 170): 51.8% used ecstasy at least monthly; 45.7% had used on more than 50 occasions; mean 4.3 years of use (SD 3.3); mean age at first use 22.0 (SD 4.9). Number of pills on a typical occasion, mean 1.9 (SD 1.0); highest number on one occasion, mean 4.7 (SD 4.0), higher in men than women (5.8 against 3.7, t(78.26)=2.78, p=0.007). Mainly oral (96.5%). Main place of use: dance parties or raves 40.8%, bars, pubs or nightclubs 40.8%, at home with others 10.7%.
exposure.polysubstance: Measured, not adjusted for. Every respondent had used at least one other substance with ecstasy. Used before, during and after ecstasy (Table 2, p. 171): alcohol 91.4%, 81.0% and 60.3%; amphetamines 60.3%, 65.5% and 45.7%; tobacco 48.3%, 62.9% and 45.7%; cannabis 36.2%, 51.7% and 62.9%; sedatives such as benzodiazepines 1.7%, 2.6% and 29.3%; antidepressants 0.0%, 0.9% and 11.2%.

comparison.controls: None (descriptive survey). Correlates compared respondents who did and did not preload, postload or change their use.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a descriptive survey; for the correlates, no adjustment of any kind (each variable tested alone).

outcomes.instruments: The authors' own questionnaire; strategies chosen from a list for avoiding (a) negative side effects, (b) the 'comedown' and (c) brain damage or neurotoxicity; open questions on changes in use and on preloading and postloading (pp. 169–170).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not validated; no pilot or reliability data reported. How often each strategy was used was not asked (p. 173).
outcomes.operationalization: A practice counts if ever endorsed (lifetime), except pill-testing frequency and preloading or postloading frequency, which were rated on a five-step scale from 'rarely' to 'always'.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Ten respondent variables (age, sex, education, years of use, frequency, more or fewer than 50 occasions, average and highest dose, recency, place of use) were tested against three outcomes (changed use, preloading, postloading); alpha 0.05, or 0.025 when normality was violated (p. 170, Data analysis). Editors' count: about 30 tests, 5 significant.

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions without intervals in the paper. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals, n=116): drinking water to avoid negative side effects 95.7% (about 90 to 98); ever preloaded 41.4% (about 33 to 51); ever postloaded 47.4% (about 39 to 56). Correlates (p. 173): preloading with younger age (24.9 against 27.6 years, t(113)=−2.59, p=0.011) and with more than 50 occasions of use (54.7% against 30.2%, chi-square 7.16, p=0.007); postloading with more than 50 occasions (60.4% against 36.5%, chi-square 6.58, p=0.01) and with use at least monthly (55.9% against 36.4%, chi-square 4.38, p=0.036). Changing use in response to dislikes with more than 50 occasions (65.4% against 42.9%, chi-square 5.80, p=0.016) (p. 171). Editors' check: all chi-square values reproduce from the implied counts as uncorrected tests; with continuity correction the frequency–postloading test gives p about 0.057.
analysis.selective_reporting: Sex differences were reported only when significant (p. 170); non-significant correlates are not listed with their statistics.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 116 respondents a prevalence of about 40–50% has an interval of about ±9 points (editors' calculation); comparisons within the 46–55 people who preloaded or postloaded are small.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 116 self-selected adults in Australia who had used ecstasy, recruited partly through harm-reduction websites in 2004, nearly all reported at least one strategy to avoid side effects (drinking water 95.7%, limiting use 70.7%, breaks 62.1%); 38.8% had ever tested pills (editors' calculation from the 61.2% who never had); 41.4% had ever preloaded and 47.4% postloaded, most often with multivitamins, 5-HTP, magnesium and fruit; every respondent had used another substance with ecstasy. Preloading and postloading were more common in respondents with more than 50 occasions of use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the results indicate that people who use ecstasy are aware of its potential for harm and actively try to minimise it (p. 168); this generalizes from a sample partly recruited through harm-reduction websites, which the authors themselves say may overrepresent interest in harm reduction (p. 173). The Discussion states that most preloading and postloading products are unlikely to cause harm (p. 174), with no data cited, and that pill testing in the Netherlands has reduced deaths, citing a newspaper report (p. 174). It calls this the first study to focus on harm-reduction strategies of people who use ecstasy (p. 173), although the Introduction describes an earlier survey of the same question (Akram and Galt, 1999; p. 169). On the other hand, the paper is explicit that the efficacy of the practices was not its focus (p. 169), that the evidence for protection comes only from rodent studies with injected pre-treatments (p. 174), that the associations are not causal (p. 175), and that some practices, such as 5-HTP with ecstasy, may carry a risk of serotonin syndrome (p. 175).

timeline.event: Sprague et al. (1994): rat study of tryptophan and 5-HTP against MDMA neurotoxicity, cited by this survey as the kind of animal evidence that may underlie preloading (p. 174); on the project's reading list, not read for this card.

Akram and Galt (1999): survey of harm-reduction practices among people using dance drugs in Nottingham, UK, as described in this paper's introduction (82% used one or more strategy; drinking water, chilling out and eating salty snacks most common; women more likely to use strategies) (p. 169).
Copeland et al. (2006), 'Ecstasy and the concomitant use of pharmaceuticals' (Addictive Behaviors), on the project's reading list; not read for this card.
Kelly (2009), 'Mediating MDMA-related harm: preloading and post-loading among ecstasy-using youth' (Journal of Psychoactive Drugs), on the project's reading list; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no later survey was read for this card. The project's reading list notes that preloading and postloading are documented only by surveys and interviews (this paper, Copeland et al., 2006, and Kelly, 2009) and that evidence of protection comes only from rat studies (Sprague et al., 1994; Aguirre et al., 1999); no human study of the efficacy or risks of these products with MDMA was found by the list's search.

funding.funder: "This research was supported by internal funds only" (p. 175, Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors from the Department of Psychology, Monash University (p. 168). Recruitment was advertised through the harm-reduction organisations RaveSafe and Pill Reports (acknowledgements, p. 175), which shapes who answered.

what_would_settle_it: For prevalence: repeated surveys of people who use ecstasy recruited with a defined frame (for example, sentinel samples at multiple sites) using standard, piloted items on water intake, breaks, pill testing and preloading or postloading, with how often each is done. For effect: controlled human studies of the products most often taken (5-HTP, magnesium, multivitamins) with MDMA, measuring objective outcomes and interaction risks.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The target is people who use ecstasy in Australia; the frame is the researchers' acquaintances, their networks and readers of two harm-reduction websites.
Convenience, snowball and self-selected web respondents; the authors note a likely interest in harm reduction among the latter.
116 gives intervals of about ±9 points for prevalences near 40–50% (editors' calculation); analyses within the 46–55 people who preloaded or postloaded are small.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex, state, education, employment, patterns and places of use, and other substances described (pp. 170–171).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Denominators vary (101 to 116) without a statement on missing answers; the counts of people who preloaded differ between text and tables; the two recruitment routes cannot be compared.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Self-report on an unvalidated, unpiloted questionnaire; strategies prompted from a list; lifetime endorsement without frequency.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same self-completed questionnaire for all respondents.
Percentages without intervals; about 30 unadjusted bivariate tests without correction for multiplicity.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: 98 questionnaires were handed out but the number returned by that route is unknown, and the web route has no denominator.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI has no overall algorithm; the editors' summary is high risk of bias for prevalence, because the sample has no frame, is self-selected partly through harm-reduction websites and has an unknown response rate, so its percentages describe these respondents, not people who use ecstasy in general. The description is careful and transparent about these limits. Cite it for what this sample reported (practices, substances used for preloading and postloading, other drugs used alongside), labelled as a 2004 convenience sample; not for population prevalence or for whether any practice works.

key_findings.finding: 116 anonymous questionnaires were returned (June–December 2004) from Australian residents aged 18 or over who had ever used ecstasy, recruited through the researchers' acquaintances and their networks (98 questionnaires distributed) and through an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter; the split between routes is unknown.

Sample: 51.3% women; age 18 to 41, mean 26.5 (SD 5.6); 79.1% had used ecstasy in the past 3 months; 51.8% used at least monthly; ecstasy was mainly taken orally (96.5%), most often at dance parties or raves (40.8%) or in bars, pubs or nightclubs (40.8%).

All respondents had used at least one other substance with ecstasy. Used before, during and after ecstasy: alcohol 91.4%, 81.0%, 60.3%; amphetamines 60.3%, 65.5%, 45.7%; tobacco 48.3%, 62.9%, 45.7%; cannabis 36.2%, 51.7%, 62.9%; cocaine 24.1%, 21.6%, 19.0%; ketamine 10.3%, 19.0%, 16.4%; GHB 8.6%, 11.2%, 9.5%; nitrous oxide 7.8%, 12.9%, 12.9%; 'amyl nitrate' 5.2%, 20.7%, 6.9%; sedatives 1.7%, 2.6%, 29.3%; antidepressants 0.0%, 0.9%, 11.2%.

Strategies endorsed from a list: to avoid negative side effects every respondent used at least one, most often drinking water (95.7%), limiting the amount of ecstasy (70.7%), a healthy lifestyle (59.5%), breaks or 'chilling out' (62.1%) and vitamins or natural products (52.6%); 30.2% took other illegal drugs and 15.5% prescription medicines for this. To avoid the comedown, 4.4% had no strategy (water 67.5%, limiting use 56.1%, vitamins 49.1%); to avoid neurotoxicity, 18.1% had none (limiting use 57.8%, water 54.3%, vitamins 38.8%).

53% had changed their ecstasy use because of what they disliked about it (the comedown was the commonest dislike, 50.0%); among these 61, 68.9% used less often, 16.4% took less per occasion, 13.1% stopped and 3.3% took more. Changing use was more common after more than 50 occasions of use (65.4% against 42.9%, chi-square 5.80, p=0.016).
Pill testing: 61.2% had never tested their pills, 16.4% rarely, 8.6% three-quarters of the time and 6% always.
key_findings.note: The abstract's 'forty percent' corresponds to 38.8% ever (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: 65.5% had heard of preloading and postloading, mostly from a partner or friends (49.4%) or the Internet (36.7%); 41.4% had preloaded and 47.4% postloaded. Preloading products (n=46): multivitamins 50.0%, 5-HTP 41.3%, magnesium 23.9%, fruit or fruit juice 23.9%, vitamin B 15.2%, vitamin C 15.2%, antidepressants 2.2%. Postloading products (n=54): 5-HTP 46.3%, multivitamins 44.4%, fruit or juice 24.1%, vitamin B 16.7%, vitamin C 13.0%, sleeping tablets 5.6%, antidepressants 5.6%, St John's Wort 3.7%.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.4, 4th paragraph (left column, continuing in the right); Table 5

key_findings.finding: Reasons for preloading or postloading (n=55): to reduce the comedown 45.5%, to reduce brain damage or neurotoxicity 32.7%, to increase the pleasurable effects 21.8%, to reduce side effects 18.2%. Frequency: 31.1% always preloaded and 28.9% rarely; 47.3% always postloaded and 20% rarely. Products came from the Internet (34%), supermarkets (32.1%), pharmacies (30.2%) and health stores (28.3%).

Preloading was associated with younger age (24.9 against 27.6 years, t(113)=−2.59, p=0.011) and with more than 50 occasions of use (54.7% against 30.2%, chi-square 7.16, p=0.007); postloading with more than 50 occasions (60.4% against 36.5%, chi-square 6.58, p=0.01) and with use at least monthly (55.9% against 36.4%, chi-square 4.38, p=0.036). No other respondent variable was significant.
key_findings.note: About 30 uncorrected bivariate tests (editors' count); cross-sectional associations, as the authors say (p. 175).

key_findings.finding: No differences between women and men in the use of harm-reduction strategies were found in this sample, unlike the earlier UK survey; men had used more than 50 times more often (60.7% against 32.2%, p=.002) and more often used in public venues (90% against 74.5%, p=0.042).

The authors state that the effectiveness of the practices was not studied, that it is unknown whether preloading and postloading reduce harm in humans, that the protective evidence comes from rodent studies with injected pre-treatments, and that taking 5-HTP, SSRIs or St John's Wort with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, last paragraph and Method 2.1 (p. 169); Discussion, 11th to 14th paragraphs (pp. 174–175)

reporting_issues.issue: The number of respondents who preloaded is not stated and the figures imply different counts: 41.4% of 116 (48, consistent with the chi-square tests), n=46 in Table 5, and frequency percentages that fit 45; for postloading 47.4% (55) against n=54 in Table 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; percentages of products refer to those who listed them, not to all who preloaded or postloaded.

reporting_issues.issue: The age comparison for preloading is reported as t(113), implying 115 respondents with data, while the companion chi-square tests use N=116; across analyses n ranges from 101 to 116 without a statement on missing answers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; missing answers are few but unreported.

reporting_issues.issue: About 30 bivariate tests (10 variables against 3 outcomes) were run without correction; 5 were significant at p from 0.007 to 0.036, and the abstract reports the significant ones as associations of preloading and postloading.
reporting_issues.consequence: The correlates are exploratory; one or two significant results would be expected by chance.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion calls this the first study to focus on the harm-reduction strategies of people who use ecstasy (p. 173), but the Introduction describes an earlier survey of the prevalence and types of such strategies (Akram and Galt, 1999; p. 169).
reporting_issues.consequence: The priority claim should not be repeated; the novelty is the focus on preloading and postloading.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 lists 'Amyl nitrate' among substances used with ecstasy; the products used as poppers are alkyl nitrites, so the label is presumably a slip for amyl nitrite.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim on the poppers page citing the 20.7% used during ecstasy should note the table's wording.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Drug Alcohol Depend 82(2), pp. 168–176 (all pages; Tables 1–6 checked on rendered pages; Figures 1–2, bar charts of frequency and lifetime occasions of use, whose values are given in the text; no supplement).
